claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar boundaries are prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
A minor Nb or similar microalloying addition will improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
The selected microalloying element has a strong tendency to segregate to and enrich interphase boundaries.
Segregation can occur during solidification or subsequent heat treatment.
An excessive microalloying addition can induce unwanted brittle second phases.
Suitable cooling and heat-treatment conditions can enable the microalloying element to diffuse to lamellar interfaces.
Boundary segregation of the microalloying element enhances interfacial cohesion.
The microalloying element may form nanoscale precipitates at lamellar interfaces.
Nanoscale interfacial precipitates can arrest microcrack propagation.
Segregation increases bonding strength at lamellar-colony interfaces.
Increased interfacial bonding reduces stress concentrations and hinders microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Suppression of interfacial microcracking increases strain-energy absorption and tensile ductility.
The modified alloy will have higher yield strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The modified alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The intervention is effective only within a segregation amount and distribution range that avoids deleterious phases and grain coarsening.
